anchors.paper_title: Electroencephalography‐Based Clustering Reveals Robust Neurophysiological Subtypes in Parkinson's Disease
anchors.reason: Same authors and cohort (116 PD patients, resting-state and treadmill walking EEG, Tel Aviv); the study paper reports recording this data, and DataCite marks it IsDescribedBy.

metadata.methods_description: EEG was recorded with a 64-channel Geodesic EEG System 400 (EGI). Participants completed about 4 minutes of eyes-open resting state while sitting and about 4 minutes of walking on a treadmill at a comfortable speed while holding the handrails. Clinical assessments included demographics, LEDD, MoCA, MDS-UPDRS and the Color Trails Test.

citation_details.title: LaBraM at Scale: Scaling Data and Models for EEG Pretraining
citation_details.author: Junyu Pan, Ruicheng Yin, Bao‐Liang Lu, Dongsheng Li, Wei-Long Zheng, Yansen Wang
citation_details.abstract: LaBraM, an early EEG foundation model, demonstrated that large-scale EEG pretraining can yield strong representations for diverse downstream tasks. Building on this foundation, we expand pretraining data and model capacity while retaining its core encoder and objective. We train ten encoders with 5.8 million to 1.97 billion parameters on three EEG collections spanning 25,067 to 79,910 hours, adapting signal preparation and training to heterogeneous recordings. Across 23 tasks, Atom-L* reaches 59.05% mean balanced accuracy at its best evaluated full fine-tuning (Full-FT) checkpoint, 3.61 percentage points above the strongest baseline EEG foundation model. Quark-G leads linear probing (LP) at 54.33%, a 1.24-point margin. Both also lead average task rank. At the last evaluated checkpoints, larger encoders improve Full-FT more consistently than LP, and stronger LP does not guarantee stronger Full-FT. citation_details.title: Attention-Guided Rest–Walk EEG Modeling for Parkinson’s Disease Classification Using CNN Features and Transformer Encoding
citation_details.author: H.M.K.K.M.B. Herath, Prathiksha Padmanabha, Nuwan Madusanka, Mailan Arachchige Don Rajitha Kawshalya, Byeong-Il Lee
citation_details.abstract: Parkinson’s disease (PD) is associated with motor impairment and altered cortical dynamics. Although resting-state electroencephalography (EEG) has been widely studied for PD classification, walking EEG remains comparatively underexplored despite its relevance to gait dysfunction. This study developed an EEG-only, leakage-free framework for participant-level classification of PD and healthy controls (HCs) using resting- and walking-state EEG data from the OpenNeuro ds007526 dataset. Following selection, preprocessing, and quality control, 132 participants were retained, including 109 individuals with PD and 23 HCs. EEG recordings were resampled to 128 Hz, filtered between 0.5 and 40 Hz, screened for artifacts, harmonized across conditions, and segmented into overlapping 6 s windows. Classical machine-learning (ML) models used participant-level engineered features, whereas deep-learning (DL) models classified pooled resting-state and walking windows. citation_details.title: Instantaneous-Frequency EEG Microstate Dynamics Stratify Motor Subtypes in Parkinson’s Disease
citation_details.author: Sou Nobukawa, Hirohisa Watanabe
citation_details.abstract: Abstract Parkinson’s disease (PD) is clinically heterogeneous, yet objective electrophysiological markers of its postural-instability/gait-difficulty (PIGD) and tremor-dominant (TD) motor subtypes are lacking. We tested whether the temporal dynamics of instantaneous-frequency (IF) microstates in resting-state electroen-cephalography (EEG) distinguish these subtypes from each other and from healthy controls (HC). In a publicly available cohort (OpenNeuro ds007526) comprising 28 HC and 97 PD patients classified as PIGD (n = 50) or TD (n = 47), the spatial distribution of the IF was reduced by principal component analysis and modeled with a Gaussian hidden Markov model, yielding three recurrent microstates. citation_details.title: Where Does EEG Help Wearable Freezing of Gait Detection?
citation_details.author: Chuntian Chi, Lifang He, Huajie Shao, Gang Zhou
citation_details.abstract: Freezing of gait (FoG) detectors built on inertial measurement units (IMUs) are accurate while the legs move, but they become unreliable when the legs are nearly still, which is exactly when akinetic freezing, voluntary stopping, and standing must be told apart. Electroencephalography (EEG) captures motor-planning activity that leg sensors cannot, but EEG is impractical for daily use. We ask where EEG helps: as an input at inference time, or only during pretraining, so that the deployed detector still needs only IMUs.
